spans.text: These times have gone, or have they?
Whatever  the  position,   clearly  the  time   has  come  when   these
instructions need sprucing up! ST-Guide has become a widely distributed
system in the  meantime, has  been completely  translated into  English
(program and docs) and  belongs to the  standard configuration of  many
home and professional Atari system users (pardon me - for some time now
also increasingly on Apples under MagiC MAC!).
Fewer and fewer authors  today are willing to  forego the inclusion  of
in the form of  a hypertext with their programs. There  are
dictionaries, subject overviews, info-booklets, legal texts and even  a
labyrinth game as ST-Guide hypertexts in addition to countless  on-line
documentation - in fact anything that can somehow be accommodated in  a
A text document receives a sort of additional dimension as a hypertext:
One can  not only  'wander'  through it  linearly in  the  conventional
manner, but also  jump 'sideways' to  other portions of  the text.  Any
character string  in  the text  can  be  marked as  a  cross  reference
'pattern' for a link. This  allows one to cross-connect related  pages,
or simply arrange them in a handy structure.
The advantage: Readers are presented with the text in small chunks with
a clear layout. In particular, if the text has been prepared  correctly
one can  reach all  chapters quickly  with a  few mouse-clicks  or  key
This leaves it up to the user  how he/she wants to read the  hypertext:
Either each page in turn from the start, or narrowly focussed  starting

Hypertexts are new. That may not seem to be so when one considers  that
they have been  available for  years, but compared  to the  traditional
form,  books,  they  offer,  besides   new  options,  a  new  type   of
presentation - for which one needs to adopt a different way of working.
In order not to make things unnecessarily difficult, ST-Guide as far as
possible adopts the way that books are structured:
table of contents and perhaps sub tables of contents

For each character input an immediate attempt will be made to find  the
in the current page; if found,
the display  scrolls  automatically  to the  corresponding  line.  This
search is a  pure text  search and  so does  not differentiate  between
marked cross references  and 'plain'  text. If  the found  string is  a
cross reference then pressing the  Tab  key (followed by  Return ) or a
mouse click will suffice to bring this up on the screen.
With the  Insert key  one can  repeat the  search for  the same  string
pattern in the rest  of the page. The  Backspace  key deletes the typed
string one character at a  time backwards, while additionally  pressing
the Shift key the clears the complete line at once.

According to the AV-documentation all  file names must be input  in
capitals with complete paths. In  order to comply with this  whilst
bearing in  mind  the called  application  doesn't know  where  the

'*:\AES.HYP' instructs ST-Guide to search for AES.HYP in all  known
A call using 'C:\AES.HYP appl_init' loads AES.HYP and displays  the
A call using 'C:\AES.REF appl_init' would search for the  reference
<appl_init> in the file AES.REF,  and if successful would load  the

A call using 'C:\AES.HYP' loads the selected file and displays  the
A call using 'appl_init' searches  for a matching reference in  the

APP -> ACC: 'A file has been dragged to one of your windows, here's
the path'. Following this ST-Guide  loads the file and displays  it
in the window. The complete path/filename must be given.
ACC -> APP: 'A key has been pressed which I can't do anything with,
so you can  have it'. This  makes it possible  to use the  keyboard
shortcuts in  an application  even if  an accessory  is the  topped
ACC -> APP: 'Start  up the program specified  in this message  with
the (possibly) specified command line'. ST-Guide uses this  message
to execute SYSTEM instructions. With Thing and GEMINI you can  also
specify non-executable files and if a program is installed for  the
given extension it will be started and the file loaded. APP -> ACC:
VA_PROGSTART, which will however be ignored by ST-Guide.
ACC -> APP: 'I've just opened a window'. Since the window's  handle
is also passed, this  serves the purpose,  among others, to  extend
window cycling of the main application  to the windows of the  ACC,
or to report to the  ACC when objects have  been dragged to one  of
ACC -> APP: 'I've  just closed one of  my windows'. Counterpart  to
ACC -> APP: 'I'm closing down - and goodbye'

ST-Guide remembers in which order one has called up which pages,
by storing them on a stack that may hold up to sixteen pages.
With the Back  icon one  can browse  back through  the pages  in
reverse order,  thus  more  or less  reversing  one's  steps  in
reaching the current page. Naturally this only works when  there
are some pages on the stack, which is not the case when ST-Guide
is first  opened, for  instance.  One can  erase the  stack,  if
desired, at the press of a mouse button. This function can  also

ST-Guide is very frugal with its mass storage requirements:
- The compiler is able to 'pack' hypertexts, i.e. reduce the amount  of
space they occupy on disk. It uses the LH5-algorithm for this,  which
also used by the LHARC packer.  In this manner hypertext files  (with
the extension HYP) can  be reduced by up  to two-thirds in size.  For
displaying the  hypertext on  the  screen the  packed pages  will  be
unpacked again without a perceivable delay.
- A further space advantage is achieved by the fact that a hypertext is
always saved as a  single file: Hypertext systems  that create a  new
file for every page (e.g. 1st-Guide) have the disadvantage that  each
of these files - be it ever  so small - always occupies at least  one
cluster of your floppy  or hard disk, which  actually means at  least
1024 bytes are consumed (more with large hard disk partitions). If  a
hypertext contains many pages whose contents are appreciably  smaller
than 1024 bytes or a multiple of this, then the actual room  required
on disk rises  appreciably because  any space up  to the  end of  the
With ST-Guide this problem  does not arise, since  all the pages  are
stored as a  single file (moreover  in compressed form),  so that  no
ST-Guide only makes meager demands on your computer's memory:
- ST-GUIDE.ACC itself is  very small, much  smaller than other  similar
- Although hypertexts are always saved as a complete file, only a small
part of this is loaded  into RAM at any time  - namely only the  page
that is  to be  displayed!  Therefore the  amount of  working  memory
occupied by ST-Guide is hardly worth mentioning.
